claim: Category-selective functional topographies are a prominent and consistent feature of lateral occipital, ventral temporal, and lateral temporal visual cortices.
source: Category-selective functional topographies are a prominent and consistent feature of lateral occipital, ventral temporal, and lateral temporal visual cortices (Downing et al., 2001; Epstein et al., 1999; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Kanwisher et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Category-selective topographies are mostly similar across individuals but are idiosyncratic in terms of their precise conformation and location.
source: Category-selective topographies are mostly similar across individuals but are idiosyncratic in terms of their precise conformation and location (Zhen et al., 2015; Zhen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research studies.

claim: Category-selective topographies and areas are typically mapped in each individual using a functional localizer fMRI scan.
source: Because of these idiosyncrasies, category-selective topographies and areas are typically mapped in each individual using a functional localizer fMRI scan (Fedorenko et al., 2010; Saxe et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional localizers map individualized topographies with simple contrasts between responses to different categories, such as contrasting responses to faces versus objects to localize face-selective areas.
source: Functional localizers map individualized topographies with simple contrasts between responses to different categories, such as contrasting responses to faces versus objects to localize face-selective areas.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about functional localizer methodology.

claim: An alternative approach to map category-selective topographies using fMRI data collected while participants view a naturalistic movie has been reported.
source: We reported an alternative approach to map category-selective topographies using fMRI data collected while participants view a naturalistic movie (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Jiahui et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: Movie data are used to calculate transformation matrices using hyperalignment that afford projecting the localizer data from the normative sample into the idiosyncratic cortical topography of new participants.
source: Movie data are used to calculate transformation matrices using hyperalignment (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Jiahui et al., 2020; Feilong et al., 2018; Feilong et al., 2021; Feilong et al., 2021; Guntupalli et al., 2018) that afford projecting the localizer data from the normative sample into the idiosyncratic cortical topography of new participants.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Naturalistic stimuli evoke a rich variety of brain states and engage multiple brain systems in parallel.
source: Unlike functional localizers, naturalistic stimuli (e.g., movies) evoke a rich variety of brain states and engage multiple brain systems in parallel.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about naturalistic stimuli.

claim: Movies better simulate real-world cognition and better engage participants' attention compared to controlled localizers.
source: Compared to controlled localizers, movies better simulate real-world cognition and better engage participants' attention (Vanderwal et al., 2015; Vanderwal et al., 2017; Vanderwal et al., 2019), contributing to more ecologically valid and higher-quality maps.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Movies are more friendly and engaging for special populations, such as young children.
source: In addition, movies are more friendly and engaging for special populations, such as young children.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the properties of movie stimuli.

claim: Response hyperalignment (RHA) requires that all participants watch the same movie to obtain time-locked responses to the same stimuli.
source: RHA requires that all participants watch the same movie to obtain time-locked responses to the same stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about RHA methodology.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment (CHA) affords calculation of transformation matrices using stimuli that are not the same for normative and index participants.
source: CHA, in contrast to RHA, affords calculation of transformation matrices using stimuli that are not the same for normative and index participants.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodological properties of CHA described in the manuscript.

claim: Four different datasets were analyzed, collected with three different movies, three different scanners, and two different types of functional localizers that used dynamic or static stimuli.
source: We analyzed four different datasets collected with three different movies, three different scanners, and two different types of functional localizers that used dynamic or static stimuli.
evidence: The claim describes the datasets used in the study.

claim: CHA based on participants' connectomes calculated using their responses to movies was able to generate high-fidelity maps of category-selective topographies within datasets that were equivalent to maps estimated using RHA.
source: We first demonstrated that CHA based on participants' connectomes that were calculated using their responses to movies was able to generate high-fidelity maps of category-selective topographies within datasets that were equivalent to maps estimated using RHA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cross-dataset predictions that used connectomes calculated from different movies for the normative and index brains were as good as those from participants in the same dataset.
source: Then, critically, we showed that cross-dataset predictions that used connectomes calculated from different movies for the normative and index brains were as good as those from participants in the same dataset.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A target participant's individualized category-selective topography can be accurately estimated using CHA, regardless of whether different movies are used to calculate the connectome and regardless of other data collection parameters.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that a target participant's individualized category-selective topography can be accurately estimated using CHA, regardless of whether different movies are used to calculate the connectome and regardless of other data collection parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Category-selective topographies estimated with CHA recovered the idiosyncrasies of individuals' topographies, capturing fine details of the individual-specific configuration and extent.
source: Category-selective topographies estimated with CHA recovered the idiosyncrasies of individuals' topographies, capturing fine details of the individual-specific configuration and extent.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A and experimental data.

claim: Topographies estimated with anatomical alignment generated highly blurred maps that were essentially the same for all participants, losing individual-specific idiosyncratic features.
source: By contrast, topographies estimated with anatomical alignment generated highly blurred maps that were essentially the same for all participants, losing individual-specific idiosyncratic features (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: In all four category-selective topographies and in all four datasets, correlations between estimations based on hyperalignment and their own localizer data were significantly higher than the correlations between estimations based on anatomical alignment and each participant's own localizer.
source: In all four category-selective topographies and in all four datasets, correlations between estimations based on hyperalignment and their own localizer data were significantly higher than the correlations between estimations based on anatomical alignment and each participant's own localizer (Fisher z-transformed, p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Predictions made with hyperalignment were close to and sometimes even exceeded the reliability values calculated with Cronbach's alpha.
source: Predictions made with hyperalignment were close to and sometimes even exceeded the reliability values (Figure 1B), which indicate that the predicted category-selective topographies from other participants' data using hyperalignment were as precise and sometimes even better than the topographies estimated with their own localizer data.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Estimates using CHA to calculate transformation matrices were equivalent to estimates using RHA.
source: Estimates using CHA to calculate transformation matrices were also equivalent to estimates using RHA (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The cross-movie predictions using CHA outperformed predictions based on anatomical alignment and were nearly as precise as within-movie predictions.
source: The cross-movie predictions using CHA outperformed predictions based on anatomical alignment and were nearly as precise as within-movie predictions (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The superior performance of cross-movie predictions was consistent across datasets and categories.
source: The superior performance was consistent across datasets and categories (p<0.001 for all comparisons, Figure 2B) and in all individual participants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and visual evidence in figures.

claim: Accuracies of cross-movie predictions matched and sometimes even exceeded the reliability measures of their own localizer runs.
source: Similarly, accuracies of these predictions matched and sometimes even exceeded the reliability measures of their own localizer runs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cross-movie predictions of cortical topographies based on different localizer types (static to dynamic or dynamic to static) produced lower correlations than did cross-movie predictions based on the same localizer type.
source: Cross-movie predictions of cortical topographies based on different localizer types (static to dynamic or dynamic to static) produced lower correlations than did cross-movie predictions based on the same localizer type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports showing significant differences between topographies estimated by static and dynamic localizers, especially in superior temporal and frontal cortices (Fox et al., 2009; Pitcher et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Searchlights in the high-level visual areas and with strong category selectivity (e.g., ventral temporal cortex, lateral temporal cortex) showed the highest mean correlation values, which often exceeded 0.8.
source: Generally, searchlights in the high-level visual areas and with strong category selectivity (e.g., ventral temporal cortex, lateral temporal cortex) showed the highest mean correlation values, which often exceeded 0.8 (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, and Figure 4—figure supplement 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The lower mean correlations in other cortices (e.g., sensorimotor cortex) reflect low reliabilities of the localizer runs.
source: The lower mean correlations in other cortices (e.g., sensorimotor cortex) reflect low reliabilities of the localizer runs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The enhanced CHA used in this study optimized the previous CHA algorithm with iterative steps.
source: We used a new, enhanced CHA in this study that optimized our previous CHA algorithm with iterative steps.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: At the final step (step 6, all vertices were used as connectivity targets) in this analysis, the enhanced CHA generated comparable performance with RHA.
source: The iterations improved the prediction performance step by step, and at the final step (step 6, all vertices were used as connectivity targets) in this analysis, the enhanced CHA generated comparable performance with RHA (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Even with just one movie run in the training or target dataset, or with a mere five participants in the training group, prediction performance (Pearson r) ranged from about 0.6 to 0.7.
source: Notably, even with just one movie run in the training or target dataset, or with a mere five participants in the training group, our prediction performance (Pearson r) ranged from about 0.6 to 0.7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The 1-step method consistently improved the prediction performances across all conditions and datasets compared to the 2-step method.
source: The 1-step method consistently improved the prediction performances across all conditions and datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The prediction outcomes were quite similar between applying transformation matrices to time series versus directly to contrast maps for both within- and across-datasets predictions.
source: Our findings indicate that the prediction outcomes were indeed quite similar between the two approaches for both the within- and across-datasets predictions (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: Using all or part of the participants for the prediction generated similar results.
source: Generally, using all or part of the participants for the prediction generated similar results (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Using only the top nine participants who are the most similar to the target participants did not significantly improve the prediction compared to using all the participants.
source: Compared to using all the participants, using only the top nine participants who are the most similar to the target participants did not significantly improve the prediction (Tukey test, z=–0.09, p=0.996), but using only the bottom nine participants generated significantly lower prediction accuracies (Tukey test, z=2.492, p=0.034).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Prior work employing diffusion-weighted imaging has underscored the link between anatomical connectivity and category selectivity across diverse visual fields.
source: Prior work employing diffusion-weighted imaging has underscored the link between anatomical connectivity and category selectivity across diverse visual fields (Osher et al., 2016; Saygin et al., 2012) and has established a notable congruence between structural and functional connectivities (Hermundstad et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The unique anatomical connectivity patterns of individuals may serve as a foundational mechanism, contributing to the stable fine-scale functional connectome.
source: These findings suggest that the unique anatomical connectivity patterns of individuals may serve as a foundational mechanism, contributing to the stable fine-scale functional connectome that underpins our approach.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited prior research.

claim: The two fine-grained connectomes based on different movies were very similar in most of the brain regions (r>0.8).
source: Results showed that the two fine-grained connectomes based on different movies were very similar in most of the brain regions (r>0.8, Figure 4—figure supplement 9A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: The across-movie connectome similarities for split halves were high (r>0.74), and the within-movie similarities were even higher in both datasets (r>0.85).
source: We found that the across-movie connectome similarities for split halves were high (r>0.74), and the within-movie similarities were even higher in both datasets (r>0.85, Figure 4—figure supplement 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9C.

claim: The fine-grained connectome was affected by the input naturalistic stimulus content, but was nonetheless highly stable.
source: Our analysis showed that although the fine-grained connectome was affected by the input naturalistic stimulus content, it was nonetheless highly stable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The dynamic localizer used short video clips for each category and the traditional static localizer used still images.
source: The dynamic localizer used short video clips for each category and the traditional static localizer used still images.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: For all categories, the dynamic localizer elicited stronger and broader category-selective activations than the static localizer.
source: For all categories, the dynamic localizer elicited stronger and broader category-selective activations than the static localizer, and the searchlight analysis showed that the dynamic localizer had higher reliabilities across the cortex, especially in regions that were selectively responsive to the target category.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The Budapest dataset included 20 participants (mean age 27.2 years, 10 females).
source: The Budapest dataset included 20 participants (mean age 27.2 years, 10 females) for this analysis.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The Forrest dataset contains scans from 15 adults (mean age 29.4 years, 6 females).
source: This dataset contains scans from 15 adults (mean age 29.4 years, 6 females).
evidence: The claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: A subset of nine participants from the original eleven participants (7 men, mean age = 24.8 years) participated in the face and object study at Dartmouth in Haxby et al., 2011, and were included in the Raiders dataset.
source: A subset of nine participants from the original eleven participants (7 men, mean age = 24.8 years) participated in the face and object study at Dartmouth in Haxby et al., 2011, and were included in this dataset.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: All datasets were preprocessed with fMRIPrep.
source: All datasets were preprocessed with fMRIPrep (Esteban et al., 2019), using version 20.1.1 for the Budapest dataset, 20.2.0 for the Sraiders dataset, 20.1.1 for the Forrest dataset, and 20.1.1 for the Raiders dataset.
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: Functional data were projected onto a standard cortical surface aligned to the fsaverage template based on cortical folding patterns.
source: After fMRIPrep, functional data were projected onto a standard cortical surface aligned to the fsaverage template (Fischl et al., 1999) based on cortical folding patterns.
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: The datasets were resampled to a cortical mesh with 18,742 vertices across both hemispheres (approximately 3 mm vertex spacing; 20,484 vertices before removing non-cortical vertices).
source: The datasets were resampled to a cortical mesh with 18,742 vertices across both hemispheres (approximately 3 mm vertex spacing; 20,484 vertices before removing non-cortical vertices).
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: Six motion parameters and their derivatives, global signal, framewise displacement, six principal components from cerebrospinal fluid and white matter, and polynomial trends up to second order were regressed out from both movie and localizer data for each run independently.
source: Six motion parameters and their derivatives, global signal, framewise displacement (Power et al., 2014), six principal components from cerebrospinal fluid and white matter (Behzadi et al., 2007), and polynomial trends up to second order were rf out from both movie and localizer data for each run independently.
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: Cronbach's alpha calculates the correlation score between localizer-based maps across the runs, and it reflects the amount of noise in maps based on individual localizer runs.
source: Cronbach's alpha calculates the correlation score between localizer-based maps across the runs, and it reflects the amount of noise in maps based on individual localizer runs.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method used in the study.

claim: Cronbach's alpha provides a more accurate statistical estimate of the reliability of the topographies estimated with localizer runs compared to split-half correlations.
source: In contrast, Cronbach's alpha involves all localizer runs and provides a more accurate statistical estimate of the reliability of the topographies estimated with localizer runs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about statistical methods.
